oil.summary: Crude staged a sharp reversal today, with Brent shedding 7.53% to $89.49/bbl and WTI dropping 6.90% to $83.15/bbl, unwinding a significant portion of the geopolitical risk premium that had built over the prior month — Brent is still +18.91% on the month. The catalyst was a halt in U.S.-Iran hostilities over the weekend, which had previously driven Brent to multi-year highs after Iran enforced a Gulf export blockade and Red Sea tanker traffic fell to a multi-month low amid sustained Houthi threats. Supply-side noise persists: at least one Saudi crude tanker has been rerouted via Suez to avoid Bab el-Mandeb, Ukrainian drones continue to target Russian refineries, and Washington temporarily eased Russia sanctions to cap prices. China's July crude imports tracking at 7.8 mb/d via Kpler provide a modest demand-side cushion. RBOB gasoline led the decline at -6.26%, while heating oil outperformed at -2.79%.
drivers: U.S.-Iran ceasefire of hostilities triggers sharp unwind of geopolitical risk premium across the crude complex
Red Sea/Houthi disruptions and Saudi tanker rerouting via Suez keep residual supply-route risk premium intact
China July crude imports tracking at 7.8 mb/d (Kpler) and temporary U.S. easing of Russia sanctions partially offset bearish pressure

gas.summary: European gas prices mirrored the oil selloff, with TTF plunging 7.67% to €58.7/MWh at the Amsterdam open as the U.S.-Iran pause eased fears of a prolonged Strait of Hormuz disruption that had underpinned a 45% monthly rally. Henry Hub was softer by 2.93% to $2.787/MMBtu, extending a -16.63% monthly slide that stands in stark contrast to TTF's trajectory — reflecting divergent fundamentals rather than geopolitical contagion. On the structural side, Japan is exploring foreign bank financing for a pledged $33 billion U.S. LNG investment tied to a bilateral trade deal, a potential long-term demand catalyst for U.S. gas. Headline flow for Henry Hub is thin today beyond the Iran de-escalation read-across.
drivers: U.S.-Iran hostilities pause drives an 8%+ TTF selloff at the open, reversing a portion of the risk-premium spike built over the past month
Henry Hub continues its own bearish trajectory, down 16.63% on the month, driven by domestic fundamentals decoupled from Middle East tensions
Japan exploring foreign bank financing for $33 billion U.S. LNG investment signals potential structural long-term demand support for Henry Hub

power.summary: Power and carbon markets saw comparatively muted moves today. EU EUAs slipped just 0.57% to $78.58/EUA, holding near one-month highs with a +3.41% monthly gain, as the gas price slump that typically weighs on carbon through reduced gas-burn economics was offset by broader geopolitical uncertainty still present in the market. The key headline backdrop for the sector includes last week's drone strike on a UAE nuclear power plant — a stark reminder of infrastructure vulnerability — and Standard Chartered's note flagging that markets must now price risk across two Middle East chokepoints simultaneously. Reports of Pakistan brokering a return to U.S.-Iran nuclear talks, strongly backed by China, could further dampen geopolitical premia if talks materialize. Direct power-sector price data is limited to TTF and EUAs today; sector-specific generation data is not available in today's feed.
drivers: EUAs resilient despite TTF selloff, with the monthly +3.41% gain holding as geopolitical uncertainty provides a floor
Drone strike on UAE nuclear power plant underscores regional infrastructure risk that keeps power-market participants on edge
Pakistan-brokered U.S.-Iran nuclear talks, backed by China, represent a potential further de-escalation catalyst that could pressure energy and carbon premia
